article.title: Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets through its "Don't Ask Again" Feature - InfoQ
article.text:
InfoQ Homepage
News
Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets through its "Don't Ask Again" Feature
DevOps
Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets through its "Don't Ask Again" Feature

Follow us on

0:00
Reading list
Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature. The company identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json intentionally committed, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos.
The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval. When developers reply "Yes, and don’t ask again" to approve a shell command, Claude Code saves it as a permanent permission rule in the local configuration file .claude/settings.local.json, which may end up inadvertently containing embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.
When [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's global git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.
On some occasions, the researchers found, Claude Code itself committed the file. Overall 63 organizations were affected, with exposed secrets including cloud API keys, production passwords and access tokens, and npm tokens. Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all exposed secrets, mostly because they were embedded inside shell commands.
The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.
The researches also note that the way Claude Code manages secrets is a security gap in itself, as to any malware "it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away", available at the same path in every project.
Apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian, which found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 of which were still valid at the time of detection, as well as another 613 in Docker Hub images. GitGuardian had previously warned that "Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history".
Commenting on the findings, Reddit user T_Thriller_T observed that "Somewhere, someone said AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles".
User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach to the whole matter of how to deal with AI files:
While this is about secrets, I totally stopped adding AI files into my projects. Means no settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or anything else. I even turned off Claude's memory. [...] Nowadays I use a memory/task/docs server through mcp and it really improved such documentation issues.
At very very least, Apiiro recommends untracking the json file using git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json and adding it to the repo's .gitignore, as well as rotating every credentials the file has ever contained. For a sounder approach, the researchers also recommend inspecting the file and deleting any rule that contains a secret, and avoid typing secrets directly into commands, referencing them instead through environment variables.

article.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows - GitHub Docs
article.text:
GitHub Agentic Workflows
Automate repetitive repository work with natural language instructions executed by AI coding agents in GitHub Actions.
In this article
About agentic workflows
GitHub Agentic Workflows are AI-powered repository automations that you define in markdown and run as GitHub Actions workflows. Unlike traditional automation with fixed if-then rules, agentic workflows use coding agents to understand context, evaluate decisions, and propose meaningful actions—all from natural language instructions.
In practice, compared with traditional workflows that execute predefined steps:
Agentic workflows execute natural language instructions with contextual reasoning.
You still define guardrails in frontmatter, such as triggers, permissions, and safe outputs.
With agentic workflows, you can automate tasks like:
Triaging incoming issues and labeling them by type and priority
Investigating CI failures and suggesting fixes
Generating daily or weekly repository status reports
Keeping documentation up to date with code changes
Improving test coverage
Benefits of using agentic workflows
Automate repetitive repository work. Define issue triage, CI investigation, documentation updates, and reporting in natural language.
Reduce workflow complexity. Write markdown instructions instead of building complex procedural scripts for every scenario.
Keep human review in the loop. Agentic workflows can generate reviewable outputs, such as issues, comments, and pull requests, while you control approvals and merges.
Run agents with layered security. Agents run in firewalled containers with read-only tokens by default. Write actions are limited to declared "safe outputs" that you have defined, and checked by agentic threat detection.
Requirements
To create and use agentic workflows, you need:
GitHub Actions enabled for your repository.
An account with an AI engine (agent), such as GitHub Copilot, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI Codex, or Google Gemini.
GitHub CLI installed and authenticated
How agentic workflows work
Each workflow markdown file has two parts:
Frontmatter (YAML between --- markers): Configures when the workflow runs, what permissions it has, and what write operations are allowed.
Markdown body: Contains your natural language instructions that the AI agent follows.
At a high level, the process to create and use agentic workflows is:
Define the agentic workflow .md file, including YAML frontmatter and markdown instructions.
Compile the markdown workflow file into a .lock.yml GitHub Actions workflow file.
Commit and push both files to the default branch of your repository.
Run the workflow like any other GitHub Actions workflow, on a trigger or in the GitHub web interface for your repository. You can also run it from the GitHub CLI.
Here's an example of a workflow to create a daily status report issue for a repository:
---
on: daily
permissions:
contents: read
issues: read
pull-requests: read
copilot-requests: write
network: defaults
tools:
github:
toolsets: [default]
safe-outputs:
create-issue:
---
# Daily Repo Status Report
Review recent activity in the repository, including issues, pull requests, discussions, and code changes.
Create a GitHub issue summarizing what changed in the last 24 hours (merged pull requests, closed issues, and new discussions), any blockers or open questions mentioned in comments, progress toward visible goals, and recommended next steps for maintainers.
Keep the summary concise. Adjust the level of detail based on how much activity occurred.
For detailed steps on creating and updating agentic workflows, see Creating GitHub Agentic Workflows.
Supported coding agents
GitHub Agentic Workflows support multiple coding agents, including:
GitHub Copilot (requires a GitHub Copilot plan)
Anthropic Claude
OpenAI Codex
Google Gemini
You specify which agent to use in the workflow frontmatter property engine. Each engine requires its own authentication secret configured in your repository. GitHub Copilot is the default…

article.title: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
article.text:
Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
OpenRouter ·11/22/2026
Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them.
These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below.
As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions:
Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations.
Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure.
Notified all potentially affected customers.
The following work is underway:
We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis.
We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties.
We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.
We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it.
Provider security announcements
Atlas Cloud: Our commitment to your security and privacy
Novita: Privacy notice regarding MiniMax requests on Novita
Phala: November preliminary incident report
Together: Security event: prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026
Not all affected providers have posted publicly. We have notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. We are encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and will keep this list updated.

hn.title: Localcode, open source agentic coding on your Mac with one command

comments.author: mark_l_watson
comments.text: Oh, this has the same name as an app I run on my 64G Mac to run deepseek 4.1 flash 10/17: https://getlocalcode.app

article.text:
Agentic coding. Local models. On your Mac.
## Install
```bash
uv pip install localcode
```
Upgrade with `uv pip install -U localcode`.
## Run
```bash
cd your-project
localcode
```
To use the running model from another local app, open `/server` or run `localcode api` for its
OpenAI compatible endpoint. See the [Local API guide](https://mjwsolo.github.io/localcode/guides/local-api/).
## What it does
- Reads and edits files in your project
- Runs your tests, builds, Git and shell commands inside the project on its own, and asks before touching anything outside it
- Searches code by name, content or structure
- Scaffolds and launches apps, then checks that they respond
- Remembers the task across messages
## Requirements
- Mac with Apple Silicon, macOS 13 or newer
- 16 GB unified memory or more
- Python 3.10 or newer
- Disk space for LocalCode and your chosen model (download sizes below)
## Models
Choose from **12 models and 169 quant options** for coding, image input and typed decisions. Models download from Hugging Face. Downloads run in parallel and can resume if interrupted. Switch with `/models`. LocalCode recommends the most capable one that fits your Mac's memory and marks it with a star.
Speed: Gemma 4, Qwen 3.6, Muse Glimmer and Qwen 3.8 draft tokens with the vendor's own speculative drafter, which downloads with the model. The model server's GPU kernels ship precompiled, so the first start after an install is quicker.
| Model | Smallest download | Largest download |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| [Gemma 4 12B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-12b-it-GGUF) | 4.7 GB | 24.3 GB |

| [Gemma 4 26B-A4B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF) | 10.4 GB | 51.0 GB |
| [Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF) | 10.5 GB | 69.8 GB |
| [Flint 40B-A2.5B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/flint-GGUF) | 11.4 GB | 79.6 GB |
| [Muse Glimmer 30B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) | 12.4 GB | 57.4 GB |
| [Gemma 4 Diffusion 26B-A4B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it-GGUF) | 16.8 GB | 50.5 GB |
| [OpenJev 27B (decisions)](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/OpenJev-GGUF) | 19.4 GB | 53.8 GB |
| [Kolibri 1 78B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Hob-forge/Kolibri-1-GGUF) | 28.6 GB | 83.1 GB |
| [DeepSeek V4 Flash 284B-A13B](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF) | 82.4 GB | 161.9 GB |
## Optimisations
What LocalCode adds on top of the stock model server to make local models faster and better at coding.
Speed
- Drafting: the vendor's own drafter guesses tokens ahead (about 2x faster replies on Gemma 4, Qwen 3.6, Qwen 3.8 and Muse Glimmer)
- Copy drafting: when the model rewrites a file it already read, it copies instead of generating (3.5 to 4x faster on rewrites)
- Prompt cache reuse: the system prompt stays the same every turn, so the model only reads what is new
- Warm-up: the first request's prompt is read while the model loads, so your first message starts sooner
- Precompiled GPU kernels: no half-minute shader compile on first start
- Threads matched to your Mac's performance cores
- Flash attention on by default
- Inkling 2: its experts run on the GPU (were silently on the CPU, about 5x slower), banded attention and a fused activation op halve its GPU memory and read prompts 20 to 30% faster
- Downloads run in parallel, resume if interrupted, and keep going while you use another model
Memory
- 8-bit KV cache by default: half the memory of full precision, so longer context fits
- Inkling 2 uses a 16-bit cache instead: its attention reads it directly, so long prompts read 1.4 to 1.8x faster and it needs 3.3 GB less memory at 128K context

article.title: ClawDOS | An AI chat and coding harness for DOS, on a real IBM PC 5160 (8088 at 4.77 MHz)
article.text:
Ricapar/ClawDOS
ClawDOS
ClawDOS
An AI coding agent for DOS.
It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.
A (real) human’s note:
Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.
It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.
I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.
From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.
Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?
And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?
I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.
As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.
Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the
files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and
looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and
picks up where it left off.
The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that
speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the
streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk.
The 8088 does everything but TLS.
See it work
Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The
conversations are with the live API.
From a sentence to a running program
One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with
Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine,
writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The
answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling,
linking and running.
The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state
and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes
back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.
WarGames, written on the XT
ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world
map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the
PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a
WG.EXE under 10 KB.
Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:
▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube
It remembers
Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS
opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY, finds the latest build, and recalls
the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.
It sees the screen

article.title: How AI is powered: a breakdown of BYOP and grid power – Better Data Center Project
article.text:
In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.
But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.1
As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.
Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site.
Figure 1. Breakdown of power source for Anthropic’s compute.
Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn”.
Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California—the world’s 4th largest economy.
This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below.
Figure 2. Anthropic’s emissions from power consumption expected in 2028. Emissions for Google, Microsoft, and Meta are annual Scope 2, location-based emissions from their most recent sustainability reports. California power sector emissions are for all power plants operating within the state (source: EIA).
Finding 3: Total CO2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO2e per year in 2028, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO2e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030.
To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO2 emissions from power use in 2028:
could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation (31.1 MMtCO2e in 2024, not including imports).
could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million, 12 million and 15 million MtCO2e, respectively)3
would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector (105 MMtCO2e).
